metadata.title: From Slow to 100x Faster: The Small Change That Transformed Our API
metadata.subtitle: When database queries slow down, use Views, Materialized Views, and Summary Tables. Learn when to use each, how to make them fast, and how to avoid common mistakes.
metadata.author: Shahid Malik
metadata.metaDescription: A practical guide to Views, Materialized Views, and Summary Tables: when to use each, performance optimization, indexing, refresh strategies, and common gotchas.

blocks.content: When your database queries start running slowly, you have three powerful tools to speed things up: Views, Materialized Views, and Summary Tables. Each one solves different problems and has its own pros and cons. This guide will help you understand when to use each, how to make them fast, and how to avoid common mistakes.
A view is a virtual table defined by a SQL query. It doesn't store data itself—instead, it executes the underlying query every time you access it.
Example

CREATE VIEW popular_posts AS
SELECT 
    p.post_id,
    p.user_id,
    p.content,
    COUNT(l.like_id) as total_likes,
    COUNT(c.comment_id) as total_comments
FROM posts p
LEFT JOIN likes l ON p.post_id = l.post_id
LEFT JOIN comments c ON p.post_id = c.post_id
WHERE p.created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'
GROUP BY p.post_id, p.user_id, p.content
HAVING COUNT(l.like_id) > 10;
Problems It Solves

items: Simplification: Write complex queries once, reuse everywhere
Security: Grant access to views without exposing underlying tables
Abstraction: Hide schema changes from applications
Always up-to-date: Queries real-time data every time

blocks.content: Drawbacks

items: Performance: Runs the full query every time (can be slow for complex operations)
No pre-computation: Can't save results ahead of time

blocks.content: A materialized view saves query results to disk. It's a snapshot that must be refreshed periodically to stay current.
Example

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW article_stats_daily AS
SELECT 
    article_id,
    DATE(created_at) as date,
    COUNT(DISTINCT view_id) as total_views,
    COUNT(DISTINCT comment_id) as total_comments,
    COUNT(DISTINCT share_id) as total_shares
FROM articles a
LEFT JOIN article_views av ON a.article_id = av.article_id
LEFT JOIN comments c ON a.article_id = c.article_id
LEFT JOIN shares s ON a.article_id = s.article_id
GROUP BY article_id, DATE(created_at);
Problems It Solves

items: Speed: Pre-computed results make queries extremely fast
Resource efficiency: Expensive calculations done once during refresh
Perfect for dashboards: Great for reports that don't need real-time data
Handles big data: Works well with millions of rows and complex calculations

blocks.content: Drawbacks

items: Stale data: Only as fresh as last refresh
Storage overhead: Takes up disk space
Refresh cost: Can be expensive on large datasets
Can block queries: Regular refresh locks the table (solved with concurrent refresh)

blocks.content: A summary table is a regular physical table that stores pre-aggregated data. Unlike materialized views, you manually control how and when data gets inserted/updated.
Example

CREATE TABLE hourly_event_summary (
    event_type VARCHAR(100),
    hour TIMESTAMP,
    total_events BIGINT,
    unique_users BIGINT,
    total_revenue DECIMAL(10,2),
    PRIMARY KEY (event_type, hour)
);

-- Incremental update (runs every hour)
INSERT INTO hourly_event_summary
SELECT 
    event_type,
    DATE_TRUNC('hour', event_time) as hour,
    COUNT(*) as total_events,
    COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) as unique_users,
    SUM(revenue) as total_revenue
FROM events
WHERE event_time >= CURRENT_DATE
GROUP BY event_type, DATE_TRUNC('hour', event_time)
ON CONFLICT (event_type, hour) DO UPDATE SET
    total_events = hourly_event_summary.total_events + EXCLUDED.total_events,
    unique_users = hourly_event_summary.unique_users + EXCLUDED.unique_users,
    total_revenue = hourly_event_summary.total_revenue + EXCLUDED.total_revenue;
Problems It Solves

items: Maximum performance: Regular table with full indexing control
Custom update logic: Full control over incremental updates and business logic
Flexibility: Add columns, indexes, constraints as needed
Mixed data sources: Combine data from multiple databases

blocks.content: Drawbacks

items: Manual maintenance: You're responsible for keeping data up-to-date
Development overhead: Need to write ETL/update logic
Data consistency risk: Bugs in update logic can cause incorrect data

sections.title: Materialized View vs Summary Table: The Critical Difference

blocks.content: On paper, Materialized Views and Summary Tables look the same—both store pre-computed data. But in production, Summary Tables are faster and more scalable. Here's why:
At SELECT Time (Read Performance)
Both are fast. Read speed is similar:

SELECT * FROM mv_org_dashboard;      -- Materialized view
SELECT * FROM org_dashboard_summary; -- Summary table
Both read stored rows. The difference is NOT here.
The Real Difference: Refresh/Update Time
Materialized View Refresh (Full Rebuild)
When you run:
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_org_dashboard;
PostgreSQL:

items: Runs the entire heavy query again
Rebuilds the whole MV from scratch
Rewrites the entire MV table
Rebuilds all indexes
Needs locks (or complex concurrent refresh)

blocks.content: Even if only 1 record changed, it recomputes everything. Full recomputation. No partial update.
Summary Table Update (Incremental)
You control the logic. You can update only affected rows:

-- Example: one new lead inserted for org_id = 'X'
-- Update only that row:
UPDATE org_dashboard_summary
SET total_leads = total_leads + 1
WHERE org_id = 'X';

-- Or recompute only that org:
UPDATE org_dashboard_summary
SET total_leads = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leads WHERE org_id = 'X')
WHERE org_id = 'X';
Partial update. Not full rebuild.
Real Production Impact
Scenario: 10 million leads, 50k organizations, dashboard refresh every 5 minutes
Why Materialized Views Become Slow Over Time
As tables grow:

items: MV refresh time keeps increasing
Index rebuild cost increases
Disk I/O spikes
Hard to refresh frequently

blocks.content: But summary table cost stays constant because you touch only changed data.
Real-World Example: Social Media Platform
Scenario: Dashboard showing most popular posts from last 30 days (50M posts, 500M likes, 100M comments)
Approach 1: Direct Query

SELECT p.post_id, p.user_id, p.content,
    COUNT(DISTINCT l.like_id) as total_likes,
    COUNT(DISTINCT c.comment_id) as total_comments,
    COUNT(DISTINCT s.share_id) as total_shares
FROM posts p
LEFT JOIN likes l ON p.post_id = l.post_id
LEFT JOIN comments c ON p.post_id = c.post_id
LEFT JOIN shares s ON p.post_id = s.post_id
WHERE p.created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY p.post_id, p.user_id, p.content
ORDER BY (total_likes + total_comments + total_shares) DESC
LIMIT 100;
Query Time: ~35-50 seconds
Approach 2: Materialized View (No Index) — Query Time: ~3-6 seconds (85% improvement)
Approach 3: Materialized View (With Indexes)
Query Time: ~0.15-0.4 seconds (99%+ improvement)
Approach 4: Summary Table (Incremental) — Query Time: ~0.05-0.12 seconds (99.7%+ improvement)
Performance Comparison

| Approach          | Query Time    | Refresh/Update Time | Improvement |
|-------------------|---------------|---------------------|-------------|
| Direct Query      | 35-50s        | N/A                 | Baseline    |
| Regular View      | 32-48s        | N/A                 | ~10%        |
| MV (no index)     | 3-6s          | 45-60s              | ~85%        |
| MV (indexed)      | 0.15-0.4s     | 45-60s              | 99%+        |
| Summary Table     | 0.05-0.12s    | 2-5s                | 99.7%+      |
Business Impact
For a dashboard with 2,000 views per day:

items: Without optimization: 2,000 × 42s = ~23 hours/day of DB processing
With indexed MV: 2,000 × 0.25s + 24 refreshes × 45s = ~23 minutes/day (98% reduction)
With summary table: 2,000 × 0.08s + 24 updates × 2s = ~3.5 minutes/day (99.7% reduction)

blocks.content: Your materialized view is a real table—treat it like one! The biggest performance wins come from proper indexing, not just pre-computing data.
Critical: Create indexes based on how people will query the MV, not the base tables.
Example: Proper Indexing Strategy

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_article_performance AS
SELECT 
    author_id,
    category,
    DATE_TRUNC('week', published_at) as week,
    COUNT(*) as article_count,
    SUM(view_count) as total_views
FROM articles
GROUP BY author_id, category, DATE_TRUNC('week', published_at);

-- Step 1: Analyze query patterns
-- Will filter by author_id? Yes
-- Will filter by week? Yes  
-- Will sort by total_views? Yes

-- Step 2: Create indexes BEFORE first refresh
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_mv_article_unique 
ON mv_article_performance(author_id, category, week);

CREATE INDEX idx_mv_article_author_week 
ON mv_article_performance(author_id, week);

CREATE INDEX idx_mv_article_views 
ON mv_article_performance(total_views DESC);

-- Step 3: Refresh
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_article_performance;
Result: Query time drops from 30 seconds to 120 milliseconds.
Indexing Best Practices
Why: Creating an index on an empty table is instant. On a populated table, it can take 10+ minutes and locks the table.

items: Filter columns: CREATE INDEX idx_mv_date ON mv_stats(date);
Sort columns: CREATE INDEX idx_mv_views ON mv_stats(total_views DESC);
Composite: CREATE INDEX idx_mv_author_views ON mv_stats(author_id, total_views DESC);

blocks.content:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM mv_article_performance WHERE author_id = 123;
Look for: RIGHT: Index Scan using idx_mv_article_author_week — WRONG: Seq Scan (add an index!)
Regular refresh locks the table, blocking all queries during refresh:

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_article_stats;  -- Takes 45 seconds
-- All queries blocked during this time!
Result: Users wait 45 seconds every refresh cycle.
PostgreSQL's concurrent refresh allows reads to continue during refresh.

items: Creates a temporary copy
Populates it with fresh data (doesn't block reads)
Atomically swaps old and new versions
Drops old version

blocks.content: You MUST have a unique index for concurrent refresh:
Advantages: No blocking - reads continue during refresh; Better user experience; Production-safe
Disadvantages: 10-30% slower than regular refresh; Uses more disk space temporarily; Requires unique index
The trade-off is worth it — slightly slower refresh is better than blocking users.
0 * * * * psql -d your_db -c "REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY mv_article_stats;"

items: High-traffic dashboards: Every 15-30 minutes
Daily reports: Once per hour
Weekly/monthly analytics: Once per day
Historical data: Once per week or on-demand

blocks.content: 1. Indexes Aligned to Read Patterns — Covered extensively above - it's the single biggest performance lever.
2. Keep Base Tables Healthy
Bloated base tables make refresh slower:
3. Simplify the MV Query
Ask: Do you really need all those joins?

-- Too complex: Multiple joins, subqueries
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_complex AS
SELECT a.article_id, au.name as author_name, c.name as category_name,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM article_tags WHERE article_id = a.article_id) as tag_count
FROM articles a
JOIN authors au ON a.author_id = au.author_id
JOIN categories c ON a.category_id = c.category_id;

-- Simpler: Only what you need
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_simple AS
SELECT article_id, author_id, category_id, view_count, comment_count
FROM articles;
4. Resource Guardrails

items: Schedule during low-traffic windows: '0 2 * * *' (2 AM)
Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to spot expensive operations
Tune work_mem for large sorts: SET work_mem = '256MB';
Set statement timeout: SET statement_timeout = '1h';

blocks.content: 5. Monitor Refresh Performance
1. Freshness Window

Staleness is a contract. Accept data that's X minutes/hours old. Decision: How fresh does data need to be? MV: Accepts 15 minutes to 1 hour of staleness. Alternative: For real-time, use streaming aggregates or incremental summary tables.
2. Refresh Cost and Ownership
Someone must own the refresh schedule, monitor it, and tune it. Set up alerts if refresh takes > 5 minutes or fails. Monitor refresh duration as data grows.
3. Storage and Backup Footprint
You're duplicating data. MV size = base query result size. Factor into disk capacity and backup windows.
4. Maintenance Surface Area
Another object to index, refresh, monitor, and document. Create runbooks for troubleshooting. Document freshness contracts for users.
When Trade-Offs Are Worth It
Use materialized views when:

items: Query performance is a bottleneck
Data freshness allows for some staleness
Refresh cost is acceptable
Storage cost is acceptable
Team can maintain the refresh pipeline

blocks.content: Don't force it if:

items: You need real-time data
Refresh would disrupt primary workload
Storage is extremely constrained
Query patterns change frequently

blocks.content: Symptom 1: MV Is Fast at First, Then Slows Down
Cause: Data growth + missing indexes. Full scans become expensive.
Fix:
Symptom 2: Concurrent Refresh Fails
Error: cannot refresh materialized view concurrently
Cause: Missing or incorrect unique index.
Symptom 3: Refresh Jobs Overlap
Cause: Refresh duration exceeds schedule interval. Fix: Use advisory locks (see Scheduling section above) or increase schedule interval.
Symptom 4: Refresh Disrupts Primary Workload
Fix: 1. Move refresh to off-peak windows 2. Simplify refresh query 3. Set resource limits: SET work_mem = '128MB'; SET statement_timeout = '30m';
Symptom 5: MV Results Surprise People
Cause: Freshness contract not visible.
Fix: Track and display last refresh time:

CREATE TABLE mv_metadata (
    mv_name TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    last_refresh_at TIMESTAMP,
    rows_count BIGINT
);

-- Update after each refresh
INSERT INTO mv_metadata (mv_name, last_refresh_at, rows_count)
VALUES ('mv_stats', NOW(), (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mv_stats))
ON CONFLICT (mv_name) DO UPDATE SET
    last_refresh_at = EXCLUDED.last_refresh_at,
    rows_count = EXCLUDED.rows_count;
Important: pg_matviews does NOT store last_refresh. You must track it yourself.
Symptom 6: Refresh Takes Longer Over Time
Cause: Base table data growth, bloat, or missing indexes.
Fix: 1. VACUUM ANALYZE base tables 2. Check base table indexes with EXPLAIN ANALYZE 3. Consider partitioning or incremental summary tables
1. Normal Views — Use when: Few reads, always-current requirement, moderate complexity. No storage, no refresh jobs, always current. Computation cost on every read.
2. Summary Tables + ETL — Use when: Incremental updates feasible, need full control. Maximum performance, custom logic, incremental updates. More work to build, manual maintenance.
3. Partitioning + Indexing — Use when: Data layout is the constraint, time-series queries. Query planner skips partitions, faster queries. Doesn't help with complex aggregations.
4. Cache Layer (Redis, Memcached) — Use when: Sub-millisecond latency needed, key-value lookups. Extremely fast, reduces DB load. Less suitable for complex aggregations.
5. Timescale Continuous Aggregates — Use when: Time-series rollups, using TimescaleDB. Automatic incremental refresh, optimized for time-bucketed data. Vendor lock-in, only for time-series.
6. Streaming Aggregates (Kafka, Flink) — Use when: Real-time aggregations, high-volume event streams. Real-time updates, handles high volume. Complex infrastructure, higher operational overhead.
Baseline Query

SELECT author_id, category, DATE_TRUNC('week', published_at) as week,
    COUNT(*) as article_count, SUM(view_count) as total_views
FROM articles
WHERE published_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '12 weeks'
GROUP BY author_id, category, DATE_TRUNC('week', published_at)
ORDER BY total_views DESC;
Time: 22 seconds
Optimized Materialized View
Query time: 150 milliseconds. Refresh overhead: 3.8 seconds (hourly)
The Math

items: Baseline: 22 seconds per query
Optimized: 0.15 seconds per query
50 queries/day: Without MV = 1,100 seconds/day; With MV = 98.7 seconds/day
Savings: 91% reduction in compute time

blocks.content: Tracking Last Refresh Time
Views, Materialized Views, and Summary Tables are powerful optimization tools:

items: Views: Best for simplification, security, always-current data
Materialized Views: Best for pre-computed aggregations with acceptable staleness
Summary Tables: Best for maximum performance and custom update logic

blocks.content: Key success factors:

items: Understand query patterns and index accordingly
Use concurrent refresh to avoid blocking reads
Monitor and maintain your materialized views
Make conscious trade-offs about freshness vs. performance

blocks.content: Remember: Index materialized views like production tables, create indexes before loading data, and always use concurrent refresh in production.
The performance gains are real: turning 22-second queries into 150-millisecond lookups is achievable with proper indexing and refresh strategies.
